Nutanix Appoints Sven Schoenaerts as Vice President EMEA, Channel and Technology Alliances
summary:
Nutanix, a leader in hybrid multicloud computing, today announced it has promoted Sven Schoenaerts to Vice President EMEA, Channel and Technology Alliances, expanding his existing channel leadership responsibilities to include technology alliances across the region. The appointment comes as Nutanix strengthens its partner-led strategy and works with its ecosystem to support growing customer demand for hybrid multicloud, modern applications and enterprise AI.
Schoenaerts, who has played a central role in the growth and transformation of Nutanix's EMEA partner ecosystem, takes on the expanded role after a successful track record of developing the company’s channel business, strengthening partner relationships, and supporting the company's regional growth. His promotion reflects the importance of the partner ecosystem to Nutanix's business and its continued investment in helping partners develop new opportunities across hybrid multicloud, modern applications and enterprise AI.
“Sven has played an important role in growing our channel business across EMEA and strengthening the relationships we have with our partners,” said Sammy Zoghlami, Senior Vice President, EMEA at Nutanix. “As customers look at how they modernise their infrastructure and bring AI into their businesses, our channel and technology partners have an increasingly important role to play. Sven has helped us build a channel organisation that works closely with partners to identify new business opportunities and deliver the technology and expertise customers need. I'm delighted to see him take on this expanded role as we continue to invest in our partner ecosystem.”
In his new position, Schoenaerts will oversee Nutanix's channel and technology alliances strategy across EMEA, with responsibility for strengthening partner engagement, developing new business opportunities and supporting the continued growth of its partner-led business. A key priority will be strengthening collaboration between channel and technology partners, developing new business opportunities and ensuring the ecosystem has the technical expertise and resources to help customers modernise their IT environments and deploy emerging technologies, including enterprise AI.
“Our partners are an essential part of how we do business, and the opportunities ahead of us are significant,” said Schoenaerts. “Customers are looking for more flexibility in how they run their IT environments, and they are relying on partners to help them understand their options and make the right decisions. I want to make sure we continue to give our partners the support, expertise and opportunities they need to grow their businesses with Nutanix. We have built some very strong relationships across EMEA, and I'm looking forward to building on those as we take the next steps together.”

Bottomline Brings USDC Stablecoin Payments Into Enterprise Payment Workflows
summary:
Bottomline, a global leader in business payments, today announced that it has completed cross-border stablecoin payments through its Global Payments Hub and Cash Management platform using USDC, issued through regulated entities[https:][1] of Circle Internet Group, Inc. (‘Circle’) (NYSE:CRCL). 
The milestone marks Bottomline's first live stablecoin transactions through its Global Payments Hub and Cash Management platform, completed as an intra-company transfer. It demonstrates how USDC payment capabilities can be incorporated into established enterprise payment workflows, enabling businesses to manage stablecoin transactions alongside traditional payment methods. 
This enables seamless interoperability between traditional and decentralised finance, ensuring cross-border and cross-chain settlement within a single platform. Stablecoin payments can sit alongside existing payment types rather than replacing them, so finance teams can choose the right option for each payment from one place. By integrating USDC into existing enterprise payment systems, Bottomline is expanding how finance teams can access these capabilities without introducing entirely separate payment workflows. 
Bottomline’s Global Payments Hub and Cash Management platform lets treasury teams manage domestic and international payments to any bank, in any currency, without logging into multiple banking portals. With stablecoins now running through the same platform, finance teams can manage digital assets alongside fiat currency and traditional payment methods, applying the same approvals, controls and audit processes they already use. For finance teams, the appeal is near real-time settlement for select payment scenarios, particularly across borders, where traditional payments need to pass through several banks before they arrive. 
“Completing our first cross-border stablecoin payments shows this is now a practical option for finance teams, not a future conversation,” said Colin Swain, Global Head of Product for Corporate Solutions at Bottomline. “Our aim has always been to make stablecoin feel like any other payment method—something treasury teams can send and track from the same place they manage everything else. The same thinking applies to the banks we work with. Their customers’ expectations are changing quickly, and they need to add new ways to pay without rebuilding what already works. Making new payment rails fit alongside existing ones is how we help businesses and banks grow at their own pace.” 
“Bringing USDC into established enterprise payment platforms is an important step toward making digital dollars more accessible to businesses,” said Spencer Spinnell, Senior Vice President, Global Payments & Enterprise Partnerships at Circle. “Bottomline's milestone demonstrates how stablecoin payments can complement existing financial infrastructure, giving treasury teams more ways to move money across borders through the systems they already use.”

French Bank Crédit Mutuel Arkéa Loses $133M Through Supplier Breach
summary:
French cooperative bank Crédit Mutuel Arkéa has confirmed it was hit by a cyber attack which saw criminals move $133 million out of the bank after they gained access through a service provider platform.
The attackers used Arkéa’s own account to send funds to other banks, where the money was converted into cryptocurrency.
The banking group, which holds €211.5 billion in assets and serves over 5.8 million customers, temporarily suspended some transactions once the attack was detected.
The theft was first reported on November 2, when blockchain investigator ZachXBT flagged more than $106 million withdrawn from centralised exchange accounts by an unnamed EU entity.
Andy Ward, SVP International for Absolute Security, commented: “Suppliers are often the easiest route in for attackers to cause huge damage to large organisations like Crédit Mutuel Arkéa. AI has shifted the balance of power towards cybercriminals in the short term, helping them to launch attacks at scale and making major breaches a case of when, not if.”
“Financial services will always be a prime target due to the money involved, but the wider concern is the growing pattern of attacks against French organisations, from supermarkets to blood banks, highlighting how cyber threats are increasingly affecting a broad range of industries and the essential services people rely on every day.”
“These attacks should serve as a warning for businesses to bolster their cyber defences, which starts with knowing which devices and supplier systems can reach their networks. Over half of CISOs reported facing a cyber breach over the past year, according to our research, with recovery costing an average of $2.5m per incident. Having the ability to recover from cyber attacks quickly and reduce downtime is vital.”
The bank has not named the supplier involved but has ruled out Fortuneo, which had been linked to the attack in the French media. The breach has been described as a sophisticated external attack and has warned customers to expect a rise in phishing attempts.
The attack follows a wave of attacks on French organisations. France formally blamed a unit of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps for October's attacks on refrigeration systems at around 700 supermarkets, summoning the Iranian ambassador and calling for EU sanctions. Refrigeration systems at three French blood-storage facilities were also targeted though that attack has not been attributed.

title: Payzone Appoints Peter O’Halloran as Chief Executive Officer
summary:
Payzone, Ireland’s largest consumer payments network, announces that Peter O’Halloran has recently joined as Chief Executive Officer, succeeding Jim Deignan, who spent 27 successful years leading the business.
Peter brings 21 years’ experience in payments and fintech across Ireland, EMEA and global markets. He most recently served as EMEA Head of Carat, the enterprise merchant business of Fortune 500 company Fiserv. There he led significant revenue and market share gain, through a combination of organic growth and acquisition. Before that, as General Manager of Global Digital Commerce at Fiserv, he built the company’s omnichannel payment gateway into a platform, serving merchants, acquirers and banks across more than 100 countries globally. Peter first worked at Payzone over 20 years ago, going on to lead its gift and loyalty portfolio. He served as a non-executive director of Payzone from 2019 to 2025 and now returns as CEO.
Elaine Downey, Chair of Payzone, said: “We are delighted to welcome Peter back to Payzone as Chief Executive. He brings extensive experience from more than two decades working in payments in Ireland and internationally, together with a strong understanding of Payzone, having started his fintech career with the company and subsequently serving on its Board.
We look forward to Peter and his team building on Payzone’s strong position as Ireland’s largest consumer payments network, with a continued focus on making payments simple and convenient for customers.”
Peter O’Halloran said: “Payzone has been part of my fintech story from the beginning. I worked with each of the company’s previous Chief Executives and I know its people, its culture and its drive to get things done. It is a privilege to return as CEO.
“As Irelald moves towards an increasingly digital, mobile, and sustainable future, Payzone’s role is more relevant than ever. I see many growth opportunities for Payzone across channels, markets, products and verticals and I look forward to working with the team and the Payzone Board, to build connected payment solutions that make daily life easier for people across Ireland.”
Peter has founded and scaled businesses throughout his career. He co-founded Branded Payment Solutions, a prepaid card business and led the launch of white-label managed services at Realex Payments. At Fiserv he served on the EMEA Executive Committee and the Global Leadership team and he was Non-Executive Chairman of Fiserv Polska S.A. He represented Fiserv on the European boards of the Merchant Risk Council and the Merchant Advisory Group and is an Ambassador for Fintech Ireland.
He holds a BA in International Business and Languages from Dublin City University and the Autonomous University of Barcelona, an MSc in Electronic Commerce from Dublin City University and a postgraduate diploma in Global Business Management from Harvard Business School.

The Payments Association Launches Payments Manifesto Setting Out UK Priorities to 2030
summary:
The Payments Association, a trade group representing the payments sector, has published The Payments Manifesto 2027, setting out a national strategy for trusted, competitive and innovative payments by 2030. The manifesto calls for payments to be recognised as critical national infrastructure, alongside sectors such as energy, telecommunications and transport.   
Aimed at government, regulators and industry leaders, the Manifesto draws on engagement with The Payments Association’s membership and has been reviewed by its Advisory Board. It builds on the Government’s National Payments Vision, setting out practical priorities to support progress towards 2030. 
The Payments Manifesto 2027: A national strategy for trusted, competitive and innovative payments by 2030 is structured around four interconnected national objectives.  
Growth, Competitiveness and Resilience focuses on modernising UK payments infrastructure through interoperability and resilience, while creating the conditions for payments businesses to grow and compete internationally.  
Trust, Security and Consumer Protection calls for earlier fraud prevention through intelligence sharing and accountability across the fraud chain, alongside improvements in financial inclusion, capability and meaningful payment choice.  
AI, Data and Digital Infrastructure seeks trusted rules for secure and accountable agentic payments, supported by internationally interoperable standards for agentic commerce.  
The future of Money and Payments calls for coherent, proportionate and internationally interoperable regulation for next-generation payments, including stablecoins and tokenised money.  
Nick Kerigan, Chair of The Payments Association’s Advisory Board and Managing Director, Head of Innovation at Swift, emphasised that payments are the invisible infrastructure of the UK economy. He highlighted that the Manifesto combines policy recommendations with The Payments Association’s commitment to convene expertise, build evidence and test proposals against real market experience. He also pointed to the Manifesto’s proposal on agentic commerce, interoperability and earlier fraud prevention as examples of how industry collaboration can help strengthen the UK’s payments sector by 2030. 
Emma Banymandhub, CEO of The Payments Association, said: “The assumption that payments can run on autopilot while facing mounting fraud and digital disruption has to end. Payments are the vital economic lifeblood keeping society functioning. If money stopped moving for even five minutes, the fallout would be significant. We aren't just presenting a wish list. Our members are stepping up to deliver the accountability, infrastructure and cross-sector collaboration required to future-proof the UK economy." 
Renuka Rawlins, Director of Policy and Government Relations at The Payments Association, commented: “The challenge now is turning policy ambition into practical progress. This Manifesto identifies where industry, government and regulators need to work together to deliver meaningful change. The Payments Association will help convene that collaboration, develop the evidence needed to inform decisions and track progress against the priorities as we work towards 2030.” 
The Manifesto’s eight policy recommendations cover the modernisation of UK payments infrastructure; international competitiveness for payments businesses; earlier fraud prevention through actionable intelligence sharing; financial inclusion and meaningful payment choice; trusted rules for agentic payments; internationally interoperable standards for agentic commerce; proportionate regulation for next-generation payments; and interoperability between existing and emerging forms of regulated money.

title: European Founders Trust AI Providers More Than Their Governments to Drive Growth
summary:
European founders trust AI providers and sales platforms more than their own governments to support their growth, according to new research from issuer processing powerhouse Enfuce.
The findings point to a trust gap at the heart of Europe's startup economy: the institutions with the most power over founders' growth are the ones they trust least.
The Startup Trust Index asked 700 founders across the UK, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the Nordics how much they trust, depend on and feel the power of 14 types of organisation, from banks and investors to software providers and government.
Key findings
37% of founders highly trust AI providers to support their growth, compared with 27% for government, the lowest of the 14 organisation types tested
Governments also rank first for power: 38% say their own government has high power over their growth, rising to 47% in the UK
56% depend on at least one type of organisation they have limited trust in, and 30% of them say the reason is lack of suitable alternatives
69% of founders use AI, and among them 56% report higher productivity and 52% better revenue or margins
Only 41% of founders are confident Europe is a good place to build and scale a business, and 39% have considered relocating, incorporating or raising outside Europe
Governments hold the power, but tech providers earn more trust 
Founders across Europe see their government as the organisation with the most power over their growth. Yet only 27% say they strongly trust it, the lowest of any organisation in the survey.
Founders put far more faith in investors and the technology and commercial partners they work with every day. AI providers and sales and distribution platforms are the most trusted, each rated highly by 37% of founders, followed by investors (35%). Other technology providers also outscore government, including business software providers (34%) and cloud infrastructure providers (32%).
The gap is biggest in the UK. Almost half of UK founders (47%) say the government has a lot of power over their growth, but fewer than a quarter (24%) strongly trust it.
AI is fuelling startup growth 
AI is becoming an established part of startup operations, with 69% of founders using it in their business, with 19% using it also for business-critical decisions and processes. One in four identify using AI as one of the developments that most supported their growth over the past year. 
Founders’ confidence in AI is grounded in ROI, with 56% reporting increased productivity and 52% reporting improved revenue or profit margins. Across all founders, 58% agree that AI presents a bigger opportunity than a threat to their business. 
Still, technology only goes so far. Almost two in three founders (63%) say the relationships they have built matter more to their growth than the technology they use.
Limited choice leaves startups reliant on partners they don’t fully trust 
More than half of founders (56%) depend on at least one type of organisation they have limited trust in. Three in ten of them (30%) say there is simply no suitable alternative. Others say the organisation gives them capabilities they can't easily get elsewhere (28%), or that the benefits outweigh their concerns (26%).
Founders rely most on sales and distribution platforms, with 35% rating their dependence on them highly. Investors (32%) and traditional retail banks (31%) come next.
What earns their trust is practical. Asked what makes them trust an organisation to support their growth, founders put value for money and keeping promises joint first (36% each), followed by being clear about terms, charges and decisions (32%).
This is the challenge for Europe's startup ecosystem. Founders need partners they can depend on, but with few alternatives, many end up relying on organisations they don't fully trust.
Growth ambitions collide with economic pressures
Operating costs were the most common barrier to growth over the past year, cited by 32% of founders, followed by economic or policy uncertainty (29%). Looking ahead, two in five founders (42%) name lower operating costs as one of the changes that would help them grow most, rising to half (50%) in the UK.
But founders aren't building just to sell. Asked what success would look like in five years, only 17% mention a sale or public listing. Far more want to build a durable, independent business, grow their revenue and customer base, or achieve financial security for themselves and their families (39% each).
“Europe’s founders trust AI providers more than their own governments to help them grow. Europe’s governments should take that seriously if they want the next generation of great companies built here,” said Denise Johansson, CEO and Co-Founder at Enfuce. “And the stakes are about to rise. AI is moving from helping founders work to making decisions, including payments, on their behalf. When something goes wrong, founders will want to know exactly who answers for it. Technology can be copied. Trust has to be earned.”

While governments hold significant perceived power over startups, they rank lowest in trust. Meanwhile, founders increasingly rely on AI and technology partners for productivity and revenue gains, highlighting a growing trust gap within Europe's startup economy.
content_ta: ஐரோப்பிய தொடக்க நிறுவனங்களின் நிறுவனர்கள் தங்கள் வணிக வளர்ச்சியை ஆதரிப்பதில் அரசாங்கங்களை விட AI வழங்குநர்களை அதிகமாக நம்புவதாக Enfuce நடத்திய புதிய ஆய்வு தெரிவிக்கிறது. அரசாங்கங்கள் தொடக்க நிறுவனங்கள் மீது அதிகாரம் கொண்டுள்ள போதிலும், நம்பகத்தன்மையில் அவை மிகக் குறைந்த இடத்தையே பெற்றுள்ளன. இதற்கிடையில், நிறுவனர்கள் தங்கள் உற்பத்தித் திறனுக்கும் வருவாய் வளர்ச்சிக்கும் AI மற்றும் தொழில்நுட்ப பங்காளிகளை நம்பியுள்ளனர், இது ஐரோப்பிய ஸ்டார்ட்அப் பொருளாதாரத்தில் வளர்ந்து வரும் நம்பிக்கையற்ற இடைவெளியை வெளிச்சம் போட்டுக் காட்டுகிறது.
